A key step, valid for Ricci solitons of every sign, is that away from the locally conformally flat case, the conformal factor is aligned with the potential function, which yields cohomogeneity-one symmetry.
Hyperelliptic curves on $(1,d)$ abelian surfaces for $d\leq 15$
Paweł Borówka; Paolo Grossi; Anatoli Shatsila

Bryan, Oberdieck, Pandharipande and Yin predicted the number of hyperelliptic curves on general abelian surfaces under a transversality condition. Some of the numbers have already been confirmed. In this paper we construct singular hyperelliptic curves on $(1,d)$ polarised abelian surfaces for $d\leq 15$ confirming a few predicted numbers, namely of (geometric) genus $g=d$ and of geometric genus $k+3$ on $(1,2k)$ and $(1,2k+1)$ polarised surfaces. Moreover, we have found that all genus 7 hyperelliptic curves on general $(1,8)$ polarised surfaces are double coverings of curves locally embedded into $(1,4)$ polarised surfaces. More interestingly, there is a unique genus 9 hyperelliptic curve (up to translation) locally embedded into a general $(1,12)$ polarised surface and it is a Klein covering of a curve locally embedded into a $(1,3)$ polarised surface.
Handlebodies separate elements of surface groups

In this note I prove that every non-trivial element of the fundamental group of a closed orientable surface X is non-trivial in the fundamental group of some handlebody with boundary X. This result appears to be folklore. I have uploaded a proof as the result is needed in a joint project with Clement Dupont on mapping class group actions on configuration spaces.
RC Prediction: A Python Package for Parameter-Aware Reservoir Computing
Jin-Cheng Rao; Zheng-Meng Zhai; Ying-Cheng Lai

A nonlinear dynamical system can be characterized by the autonomous evolution of its state in time and its dependence on system parameters. As a parameter varies, the dynamics can change quantitatively and, at bifurcation points, qualitatively. When the governing equations are unknown, a data-driven model should therefore capture both elements from observational data, rather than reproduce the dynamics at a single operating condition only. Parameter-aware reservoir computing (PARC) is a model-free framework for this purpose, where the parameter is supplied to a reservoir computer through an additional input channel. PARC is trained on time series recorded at several parameter values, and the trained reservoir, run in closed loop as an autonomous dynamical system, generates trajectories at parameter values that were never observed. rc_prediction is an open-source Python package that implements this workflow. It provides multi-parameter training of a reservoir, autonomous closed-loop prediction at user-specified parameter values, parameter scans, and a standard echo state network for forecasting at a fixed parameter. Hyperparameter optimization and optional GPU acceleration through PyTorch are also provided. We use three benchmark dynamical systems as examples to demonstrate its usage. As one of the featured applications, here we illustrate the prediction of critical transitions and system collapse: trained only on pre-critical data, the model is queried beyond the training range to predict whether the system collapses, to estimate the critical parameter $p_c^{*}$, and to characterize transient lifetimes.
Martingale Representation in Counting-Process Filtrations via Poisson Embedding
Caroline Hillairet; Thibaut Mastrolia; Anthony Réveillac

We revisit martingale representation for counting processes using the Poisson embedding, deriving the representation in their natural filtration from that of the underlying Poisson random measure. Our approach combines Poisson Malliavin calculus with the Clark-Ocone and Mecke formulas. We first characterize measurability with respect to the counting-process filtration through the structure of the Malliavin derivative. We show that any random variable measurable in the counting-process filtration is invariant with respect to the auxiliary mark on the acceptance region obtained from the Poisson embedding method and vanishes on the rejection region. We then prove that every square-integrable martingale in this smaller filtration consequently admits a unique stochastic integral representation with respect to the compensated counting process: the integrand is explicitly characterized as the conditional expectation of the Malliavin derivative, which identifies as the conditional effect of an additional accepted event on the terminal functional. Additionally, we define the mirroring counting process which counts the rejected events in the Poisson embedding procedure and we then provide an orthogonal decomposition of any martingale in the joint filtration of the accepted and rejected counting processes as a sum of a martingale in the counting filtration obtained by Poisson embedding and its mirroring martingale part on the rejected domain. Finally, we apply these results to general Hawkes processes constructed by Poisson embedding, obtaining a martingale representation and an explicit integrand formula in their natural filtration.
Connes spectral distance as a quantum distance measure and a geometric measure of entanglement

In this paper, we study the Connes spectral distance as a quantum distance measure and its applications in discriminating quantum states and calculating quantum entanglement. Based on finite matrix algebra, we construct a spectral triple for finite dimensional quantum states. The Connes spectral distance is a generalization to the quantum trace distance and Hilbert-Schmidt distance. The corresponding optimal elements can always be chosen to commute with the difference matrix $Δ$, and then the optimal element and $Δ$ can be simultaneously diagonalized. We obtain the formulas of Connes spectral distances in three different parameter regimes which depending on the spectrum of difference matrix. As applications, we show how to use spectral distances to distinguish state pairs that have the same trace distance and Hilbert-Schmidt distance. We also define a new geometric measure of entanglement based on spectral distance. These results can help us study the relationships among Connes spectral distance, quantum trace distance and other quantum distance measures. These concrete constructions are significant for studies of quantum states in the framework of noncommutative geometry.
Existence and stability of Weyl points

Weyl points are quasimomentum-energy pairs in the band structure of three-dimensional periodic media at which two dispersion surfaces touch conically. They first arose in a model introduced by H. Weyl in 1929, but were first observed only recently in condensed matter physics and photonics experiments. Weyl points have been explored theoretically via numerical computation and via tight binding (discrete) models. In this article we present the first analytical treatment of Weyl points in a continuum PDE-type model. Starting with a Schrödinger operator whose electric potential is periodic with respect to the body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice, we introduce a small BCC-periodic magnetic vector potential that is equivariant with respect to a specific abelian group of symmetries. For magnetic Schrödinger operators of this type, we prove (i) that a pair of Weyl points bifurcates from a threefold degeneracy in the band structure of the underlying non-magnetic operator, and (ii) that these Weyl points are stable against small self-adjoint BCC-periodic perturbations of both the electric and magnetic vector potentials.
Isometric Embeddings of Asymptotically Hyperbolic Manifolds into Hyperbolic Space

The Nash Embedding theorem asserts that every closed Riemannian manifold can be isometrically embedded into a Euclidean space of sufficiently high dimension. In this paper, we address the asymptotically hyperbolic version of the problem. We prove that an asymptotically hyperbolic manifold $\left(M,g\right)$ can be realized as a submanifold of a sufficiently high-dimensional hyperbolic space $\mathrm{H}^{N+1}$, intersecting the sphere at infinity transversely, if and only if $g$ is asymptotically Poincaré-Einstein to second order.
Nondegeneracy of low-energy nodal solutions to the Yamabe equation
Sérgio L. N. Neves; Angela Pistoia

We study the linearized Yamabe equation in $\R^n$, or equivalently on $\s^n$, at a low-energy sign-changing solution with two nodal domains. We consider odd dimensions $n=2k-1$ and a solution invariant under $Γ=O(k)\times O(k)$. Its regular level sets are isoparametric hypersurfaces, which foliate the sphere away from the two focal submanifolds. This symmetry reduces the equation for the solution to a singular ODE. In the balanced case, we choose a single-node profile that is odd under reflection across the midpoint. We prove nondegeneracy in the $Γ$-invariant subspace for every $k\ge2$, and in the full space $H^1(\s^n)$ for sufficiently large $k$: every kernel element is generated by a conformal invariance of the equation. The proof uses separation of variables, Wronskian identities and comparison functions adapted to the singular equations for the angular modes.
On lens spaces which may embed in the complex projective plane

Using an obstruction derived by Owens and relying on Donaldson's Diagonalisation Theorem, we obtain a complete classification of lens spaces of Lisca type $(2)$ or $(3)$ that are unobstructed from embedding in a homology complex projective plane. This classification is further refined for lens spaces $L(p,q)$ with $p$ even, using an obstruction due to Lidman--Moore--Vazquez based on work of Lin. This article is extracted from the author's PhD thesis.
Scientist Mothers Working in Childcare Deserts Are Less Likely to Attain Tenure

Childcare shortages have limited families' access to quality care, with consequences for children's development and parents' careers. We link two decades of childcare supply data to longitudinal surveys of U.S. scientists. We find workplace childcare deserts are widespread: more than half of scientists at universities and research institutions work in deserts, where supply falls significantly short of demand. We further find mothers working in deserts are less likely to attain tenure. They are also more likely to move to industry and part-time positions. Reduced work time partly accounts for the tenure association but other reasons remain. Expanding childcare availability near workplaces may help retain scientific talent.
Uniformization of compact Kähler Threefolds of Zero Kodaira Dimension
Given two smooth compact Kähler threefolds $X$ and $Y$ whose universal covers are biholomorphic, we show that $κ(X) = 0$ if and only if $κ(Y) =0$.
Kernel-based Interpolatory Methods for Context Compression of Attention Mechanisms

The bottleneck of attention mechanisms, which are the fundamental building block of modern language models, is their quadratic complexity in terms of context size. There has thus been an increasing interest in the compression of the context, also called KV-cache compression. In this article, we consider the problem of compressing the context of attention mechanisms by first formulating it in the Hilbert space associated with its kernel. In this formalism, attention can be represented as the ratio of two linear maps whose interpolant is also the ratio of interpolants, this allows us to consider the interpolation of the linear maps directly. We thus introduce two novel KV-cache compression methods which we call GAIM and Q-DAIM, based on the Generalized Empirical Interpolation Method (GEIM) and the Q-Discrete Empirical Interpolation Method (Q-DEIM), respectively. As the cost of these methods is quadratic in terms of context length, we propose surrogate models based on the Taylor series, the Performer and the Random Fourier Features method which allow the compression to be done in linear time. Finally, we extend this result to the streaming attention setting, providing new methods which allow one to penalize the selection of interpolation nodes based on the previously interpolated context and to update the previous interpolation based on new information. We then provide numerical results on the convergence of the residuals and the output error in future queries and preliminary results on the LongBench-E benchmark showing performance comparable to the state-of-the-art methods. These experiments suggest that the range revealed by our Q-DAIM method could help identify where information is concentrated in the KV cache, thus enabling an efficient compression.
Immersed Boundary Electrodiffusion in the Wasserstein Gradient Flow Formalism: Global Well-Posedness, Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics, and Singular Asymptotics

We introduce a unified optimal transport framework for the Immersed Boundary (IB) electrodiffusion active pump model. By representing membrane chemical potential barriers and active pump potentials via smoothed Eulerian kernels ($Ψ_w, \mathcal{H}_w$), we formulate the passive dynamics as an $L^2$-Wasserstein ($W_2$) gradient flow coupled to non-conservative active pushing fields representing ATP-driven $3:2$ $\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+$ exchangers. We establish global weak existence of solutions to the continuous Poisson--Nernst--Planck--IB system via a split-step Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto (JKO) variational scheme, backed by Calderón--Zygmund bounds for non-local Poisson drift and $H^3(\mathbb{S}^1)$ interface regularity under Stokes flow. We prove the continuous Rayleighian energy balance and establish exponential $W_2$-stability of Non-Equilibrium Steady States (NESS) under a quantitative Bakry--Émery curvature threshold. Furthermore, we analyze the dual singular limits of kernel smoothing width $w \to 0$ and dimensionless Debye length $g = λ_D / L \to 0$. We establish the precise asymptotic regime connecting regularized and sharp models, prove the $Γ$-convergence of regularized energy functionals, derive distributional interface flux jump conditions, and resolve $O(λ_D)$ Debye space-charge boundary layers to confirm bulk electroneutrality.
Learning Stabilizing Latent Feedback Controllers via Multi-Step Backward Losses
Paul Lutkus; Lars Lindemann; Stephen Tu

Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.
Scaling Limits as Extensions of Continuous Bundles of C*-algebras

We analyze scaling limits in algebraic quantum field theory using continuous bundles of C*-algebras. Different conditions of continuity on such bundles encode different strengths of approximation of the theory by its scaling limit. As a proof of concept, we consider the small-distance scaling limit of the theory of a massive free scalar field, which corresponds to a massless free scalar field. We provide a number of examples of local algebras of observables for which the corresponding bundle of C*-algebras representing the scaling limit is merely lower semicontinuous. Further, we construct an algebra of nonlocal observables for which the corresponding bundle of C*-algebras representing the scaling limit is uniformly continuous.
Spectral Convergence of the Discrete Steklov Problem

We study the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Schur complement $\textbf{S}$ of the graph Laplacian, defined on vertices sampled from a domain with $C^2$ boundary. We use a thin boundary layer to approximate the continuum boundary as the number of vertices increases and rely on transportation theory to justify the consistency of a discrete Steklov problem. In particular, $\textbf{S}$ acts on vectors defined over the shrinking boundary layer but behaves asymptotically like a known operator. In this paper, we use a variational argument to determine conditions for which the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $\textbf{S}$ converge to the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map, and we provide evidence of this spectral convergence through a numerical example.
Fast and Accurate Hydro Unit Commitment
Shaked Regev; Evan J. R. Brody

We introduce a fast novel algorithm to commit hydro-generators. We show that our algorithm can commit 56 generators for 200 days 10,000 times faster than Hexaly, the leading commercial solver for scheduling problems, without sacrificing solution quality. Our method can commit 1792 generators for an entire year in approximately 20 seconds on commodity hardware. Hexaly is unable to solve problems of this size in reasonable time. We attain this runtime improvement by introducing a greedy-heuristic tailored for hydro units. We provide a direction for a possible proof that the error our solver makes decreases with the problem size. This is supported by our experimental results. We prove that our solver's runtime scales log-linearly in the number of generators and time periods.
Higher limits over the fusion orbit category via subgroup complexes

Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a saturated fusion system over a finite $p$-group $S$, and $\mathcal{O}^c (\mathcal{F})$ denote the centric orbit category of $\mathcal{F}$. Suppose that $G$ is a discrete group realizing $\mathcal{F}$, and $\mathcal{C}$ is the collection of all $p$-centric subgroups in $G$. We prove that for every $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)} \mathcal{O} ^c (\mathcal{F})$-module $M$, the higher limits $\lim ^* _{\mathcal{O}^c (\mathcal{F})} M$ are isomorphic to the equivariant cohomology $H_ G ^* (|\mathcal{C}| ; \mathcal{M} )$, where $\mathcal{M}$ is the $G$-equivariant coefficient system on $|\mathcal{C}|$ induced by $M$. This is the fusion system version of a theorem by Grodal for higher limits over the $p$-orbit category $\mathcal{O}_p(G)$ of a finite group $G$. As a consequence, for every fusion system $\mathcal{F}$, we obtain a finite sequence of cohomology groups, involving the cohomology of $\mathcal{F}$, which is exact if and only if the mod-$p$ subgroup decomposition for $\mathcal{F}$ over $\mathcal{F}$-centric subgroups is sharp.
Global Testing of Gaussian Means by Combining Marginal and Conditional Evidence
Deepra Ghosh; Edgar Dobriban; Sanat K. Sarkar

We propose a test of the global null hypothesis of zero means in correlated multivariate Gaussian data by combining marginal and conditional evidence at each coordinate. The conditional tests are based on the distribution of each coordinate given the remaining coordinates. At each coordinate, the corresponding two-sided $p$-values are combined using the Simes method, followed by a Bonferroni correction across coordinates. Because conditioning can either strengthen or weaken evidence against the null, neither marginal nor conditional testing is uniformly preferable. The proposed procedure adapts to their relative strengths while retaining the simplicity of minimum-type global testing. We establish finite-sample control of the global Type-I error under both known covariance and covariance estimated from an independent sample. The latter setting requires a careful analysis of the dependence between studentized marginal and conditional statistics. We evaluate the power of the proposed test through simulations, compare its performance with existing global tests, and illustrate its practical utility using a TCGA carcinoma dataset.
Global strong solutions of the three-dimensional Cahn--Hilliard--Navier--Stokes system via finite-dimensional scalar forcing
Víctor Hernández-Santamaría; Subrata Majumdar; Yingying Wu-Zhang

In this paper, we establish global existence of strong solutions for the three-dimensional Cahn--Hilliard--Navier--Stokes system on the torus through finite-dimensional scalar modifications of a prescribed external force. For arbitrary initial data in $H^1\times H^2$ and any force that is locally bounded in time, we construct two smooth scalar corrections, one added to the third component of the fluid force and the other to the phase source. These corrections involve three fixed Fourier frequencies in the fluid equation and one in the phase equation, and act only on a set of times of arbitrarily small total measure. The proof combines a quantitative local theory with repeated returns of the solution to a fixed ball around zero. These returns rely on small-time asymptotic limits that balance the different scales of the two equations, together with a saturation procedure carefully adapted to the structure of the coupled system. Fluid transport generates the phase frequencies that the chosen phase forcing cannot produce on its own. As a consequence, we also obtain global strong solutions for the three-dimensional Navier--Stokes equations with a single smooth scalar correction acting on one component of the force at three fixed Fourier frequencies.
Incremental Stability of Gradient Flows under Generalized Polyak-Łojasiewicz Inequalities and Its Implications for General Systems
Andreas Oliveira; Arthur C. B. de Oliveira; Mario Sznaier; Eduardo Sontag

Gradient flows of twice continuously differentiable strongly convex and convex objectives are, respectively, incrementally exponentially stable and non-expansive in the Euclidean metric. In this work, we investigate to what extent these properties extend to nonconvex objectives satisfying generalized Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequalities. For objectives with a unique minimizer, we establish conditions under which the gradient flow is contracting in a state-dependent Riemannian metric and incrementally exponentially stable. For objectives with nonunique minimizers, we generalize the non-expansivity of convex objectives to incremental stability for more general nonconvex objectives. We focus on incremental stability due to its implication to convergence to equilibrium points; when paired with a Lyapunov function it implies pointwise convergence to a minimizer and continuity of the endpoint map. Along the way, we derive new structural results for incrementally stable nonlinear systems and extend the analysis to Heavy-Ball and Dynamical Inertial Newton flows.
Equivariant Gradient Degree Comparison via Clarke Duality for Strongly Indefinite Hamiltonian Systems

We study equivariant gradient degree comparisons for strongly indefinite Hamiltonian systems through Clarke duality. Under suitable convexity and compactness assumptions, we establish a correspondence between the primal and dual equations that preserves the symmetries of their solutions. We derive an identity relating their negative spectral representations and show that the Galerkin-normalized local index of the primal linearization coincides with the equivariant gradient degree determined by the dual Hessian. This comparison extends to infinite-dimensional settings through stabilized Galerkin approximations. We also establish relations between primal and dual crossing forms, equivariant spectral flow, and local equivariant gradient degrees at nondegenerate fixed solutions. The results provide a framework for studying equivariant bifurcation in strongly indefinite systems. As an application, we consider periodic Hamiltonian ring equations with dihedral symmetry and illustrate the computation of equivariant gradient degrees and bifurcation invariants.
Basis statistics for phylogenetic tree shape: tree balance formulas beyond expectations
Daniel J. Bauman; Noah A. Rosenberg

Summary statistics that measure the shapes of phylogenetic trees contributed to quantitatively understanding evolutionary processes. Among phylogenetic summary statistics, the tree balance indices have been designed to capture intuitive notions of balance or imbalance in trees. Here, we characterize the tree balance indices in terms of basis statistics, mapping the exponentially large space of rooted, binary, unlabeled trees to lower-dimensional spaces. We observe that many tree balance indices can be represented in terms of linear functions of these low-dimensional spaces, enabling us to compute exact formulas for the means, variances, and covariances of many balance indices under the Yule--Harding model. The new framework recapitulates existing formulas for the expectations of 8 indices: Sackin index, average leaf depth, total cophenetic index, $\hat{s}$-shape statistic, Colless index, corrected Colless index, quadratic Colless index, and rooted quartet index for binary trees. It produces new formulas for the expectations of 9 additional indices: equal weights Colless index, total $I$ index, total $I'$ index, Rogers $J$ index, total internal path length, total path length, average vertex depth, stairs1 index, and stairs2 index. Moreover, the framework also allows us to calculate the exact variance of all 17 indices that are represented by the bases as well as the covariance and correlation for all $\binom{17}{2} = 136$ pairs among the 17 indices.
Truncated Grassmannians: polytopes, representations, and Cauchy formulas

The goal of this paper is to develop algebraic and combinatorial techniques for studying the geometric properties of truncated Grassmannians, a class of algebraic varieties obtained via certain projections of classical Grassmannians within their Plücker embeddings. We introduce a class of cyclic representations of maximal parabolic subalgebras of the general linear Lie algebra, which are proved to serve as duals of the homogeneous components of coordinate rings of truncated Grassmannians. We prove that the characters of these representations are computed via truncated Cauchy formulas and establish a connection with coordinate rings of complete collineations. We also construct monomial bases of these representations in terms of certain generalized chain polytopes and use the RSK correspondence to establish connections with Cauchy-type formulas and with Gelfand--Tsetlin patterns.
Some properties of completely convex functions

We study the class $CC_α$ of completely convex functions of order $α$, defined through a two-point analogous of the classical convexity condition. We give several equivalent characterizations of $CC_α$, together with representation formulas in terms of two auxiliary Schwarz functions linked by a compatibility equation. From these representations, we derive coefficient bounds, a subordination result $zf'/f$, and a two-point Taylor expansion in which the Schwarzian derivative $S_f$ arises naturally as the coefficient of the linear term. This yields a pointwise bound for $S_f$ and a bound for the pre-Schwarzian norm $\|P_f\|_{CC_α}$, improving the classical Yamashita bound when $α\leq 1-1/\sqrt2 $. We also show that, unlike the class $C_α$ of convex functions of order $α$, every $f\in CC_α$ is bounded when $α>0$.
Addendum to "Optimal Steering of a Linear Stochastic System to a Final Probability Distribution, Part II"
Yongxin Chen; Tryphon T. Georgiou; Michele Pavon

We hereby fill in a gap in an induction argument used in the proof of a theorem on state-covariance controllability of linear stochastic systems in an earlier paper by the authors. The mathematical statement is true. The missing point in the proof concerns the assertion that, in the canonical single-input case, the control can be assigned arbitrary endpoint values. We amend the argument by proving a slightly stronger induction statement that permits arbitrary finite endpoint jets of the control. An independent approach to homogeneous state-covariance controllability was provided in a paper by Abdelgalil and Georgiou (2025) as a corollary of strong controllability results on $\GLp(n,\mathbb R)$, and shown herein that it extends to the case of additive noise as well.

Using a unified method of identifying a telescoping function for each statistic-action pair, we prove conjectures of La Croix and Roby, and of Sheridan-Rossi that various permutation statistics, such as the number of fixed points, are homomesic under Foatic actions: compositions of the Foata bijection and dihedral symmetries of one-line notation. Underlying these results is a family of bijective identities relating permutation statistics across the Foata bijection; one of them --- an unexpected invariance of the number of right-to-left minima under reverse-complement, proved by an explicit bijection --- may be of independent interest. The telescoping functions also turn out to be shared among some Foatic actions, implying that mixing certain actions still yields a constant average on closed walks.
Quantitative Stability for Anisotropic Gaussian Isoperimetric Inequality

We prove a sharp, dimension-free quantitative stability theorem for the Gaussian isoperimetric inequality in general Gauss spaces $(\mathbb{R}^n,γ_A)$, where $A$ is an arbitrary positive-definite matrix. More precisely, we show that the anisotropic Gaussian perimeter deficit controls the square of the anisotropic Gaussian asymmetry with a dimension-free constant, recovering the sharp quadratic stability behavior known in the isotropic setting. The central difficulties are the loss of rotational symmetry and the lack of compactness of the isoperimetric sets. The main novelty of our work is a new symmetrization-based reduction to the small-perturbation regime, together with effective Fuglede-type estimates derived from the weighted constant mean curvature equation. These ingredients overcome the principal obstructions created by anisotropy and extend the proof-from-regularity approach to quantitative isoperimetric stability in the anisotropic setting.

We prove an entropic $c$-theorem in two dimensions by constructing a $c$-function from the mutual information between spacelike separated wedges, defined through the relative entropy. The proof follows Casini and Huerta's, with strong subadditivity of entanglement entropy replaced by increasing differences of the mutual information, which we prove directly in the continuum from the split property and standard properties of relative entropy. The benefit of relative entropy is that every quantity we use is finite and no cutoff ever needs to be introduced. The assumptions of the theorem are only the standard axioms of algebraic quantum field theory, the split property with finite mutual information across a gap (both implied by modular $p$-nuclearity), and a finite ultraviolet bound on the resulting $c$-functions. We also note that, formally, the $c$-function is proportional to the minimal averaged null energy of a state that reproduces the vacuum correlations between the two wedges.
On the estimation of the Gromov-Hausdorff distance

The paper investigates the Gromov--Hausdorff distance using a new tool, the so-called $\varkappa$-traces of metric spaces. A general lower bound for the Gromov--Hausdorff distance is obtained in terms of $\varkappa$-traces. Using this bound, exact estimates for the distance between an arbitrary metric space and its Hausdorff hyperspace are derived, and the behavior of the metric on transfinite towers (inductive limits) of hyperspaces is studied. In the final part of the paper, the trace machinery is applied to $l^p$-products of metric spaces. A connection is established between computing the Gromov--Hausdorff distance for infinite $l^\infty$-products and partition calculus. Using methods from Ramsey theory (in particular, the Erdos--Rado theorem), $\varkappa$-traces for $l^\infty$-products are computed, and sufficient conditions are obtained under which the Gromov--Hausdorff distance between infinite Cartesian products can be computed exactly. The final section also provides a general estimate for the Gromov--Hausdorff distance between $l^\infty$-products of metric spaces using the Erdos--Rado theorem.
Simple Cuts, Simple Landscape: Dimension-Free Rank Bounds for Burer-Monteiro Factorizations via Rank-Width

In this work, we study Burer-Monteiro factorizations of semidefinite programs with unit diagonal constraints. For a real symmetric cost matrix whose rank-width over $\mathbb{R}$ is at most $k$, we prove that every non-flat second-order stationary point of the factorized problem is globally optimal whenever the factorization rank is at least $2k$, independently of the matrix size.

We propose a phenotype-structure form of the Cahn-Hilliard equation with degenerate mobility and analyze the existence of weak solutions for this new variant. This model is motivated by tumor modeling as multiple phenotypes co-exist within the same tumor and are believed to constitute a continuum of phenotypes. The originality of the model lies in its ability to consider an infinite number of phases and it allows for spatial interactions between phenotypes as well as transport in the phenotypic space, i.e., mutations.
Short Jennings series and the modular isomorphism problem

Let $p$ be an odd prime and $G$ a finite $p$-group whose Jennings series has length at most $p$, that is, $D_{p+1}(G)=1$; when $D_p(G)\ne1$ assume also that $G/D_p(G)$ has nilpotency class at most $p-2$. We prove that $G$ is determined up to isomorphism by its modular group algebra $\mathbb{F}_p G$, and indeed by the quotient $\mathbb{F}_p G/\mathrm{I}^{\,ν+1}$, where $\mathrm{I}$ is the augmentation ideal and $ν$ the length of the Jennings series; for an arbitrary finite $p$-group $G$, the quotient $\mathbb{F}_p G/\mathrm{I}^{\,p}$ determines $G/D_p(G)$; and that every automorphism of $\mathbb{F}_p G$ is the product of an automorphism of $G$ and an automorphism inducing the identity on $\mathrm{I}/\mathrm{I}^2$. In particular the modular isomorphism problem has a positive answer for all $p$-groups of exponent $p$ and class less than $p$, and for all $p$-groups of class at most $p-2$ and exponent dividing $p^2$ whose derived subgroup has exponent $p$. Consequently every counterexample in odd characteristic has class at least $p-1$, or a derived subgroup of exponent at least $p^2$, or an element of order $p^3$. The proof combines a descent theorem in the truncated group algebra of a free group, valid for every prime, with a relative rigidity theorem for the unipotent automorphisms of truncated group algebras of groups of exponent $p$, proved through the Lazard correspondence. The bound $p$ is the range in which the logarithm of the group algebra exists.
Analysis of Triggered Packet Streams: Stochastic Bounds on System Time under General Triggering Delays
Mehran Rahnamania; Michel Mandjes; Farid Ashtiani

Many emerging communication systems increasingly involve devices that transmit packets in multiple causally dependent stages as part of an internal workflow, rather than waiting for receiver feedback. To analyze such systems, we recently introduced the $\mathrm{M^T/G/1}$ queue, in which primary customers arrive according to an exogenous Poisson process, and each triggers a secondary customer to join the queue after an independent random delay, called the \textit{triggering delay}. Our prior heuristic approximations assume identical exponential service times, and our matrix-analytic framework assumes exponential triggering delays. However, no exact analysis is available when both distributions are general. In this paper, we derive stochastic bounds, in the usual stochastic order, on the system-time distribution of each customer class under general triggering-delay and service-time distributions. The service times within each primary--secondary pair may be generally dependent. Using sample-path coupling and level-crossing arguments, we show that the stationary workload is stochastically sandwiched between those of two classical queues: a two-class $\mathrm{M/G/1}$ queue with independent Poisson arrivals (lower bound), and a batch-arrival $\mathrm{M^{[2]}/G/1}$ queue where each primary--secondary pair arrives simultaneously (upper bound). Notably, these bounds do not depend on the triggering-delay distribution, and they are asymptotically tight in the sense that the stationary workload converges in distribution to that of the lower- and upper-bound queues as the triggering delays diverge to infinity and converge to zero in probability, respectively. We translate these workload bounds into system-time bounds for each customer class. Simulation experiments support these bounds.

Let $A$ be a finite abelian group. A nowhere-zero $A$-flow of a graph gives every edge a direction and a non-zero value in $A$, so that at every vertex the sum of the values on the entering edges equals the sum on the leaving edges. Such a flow can be changed along a cycle: going around the cycle, add a fixed non-zero element of $A$ to the value of every edge that points forward and subtract it from the value of every edge that points backward. The Cranston--Li--Su--Wang--Xu (2026) conjecture states that if $A$ has at least four elements, then in every graph in which all degrees are even, any two nowhere-zero $A$-flows are joined by a chain of such changes through nowhere-zero $A$-flows. It also states that, for every integer $k\ge 4$, the same holds for integer flows whose values are between $1$ and $k-1$ in absolute value, where each change adds a non-zero integer. We prove this conjecture. The core of the proof is an induction on the number of edges: if a flow enters a vertex $v$ along an edge $uv$ and leaves $v$ along an edge $vw$ with the same value, the two edges can be replaced by one edge $uw$, and the induction hypothesis applies to the smaller graph. So the main task is to change every flow into a flow with such a pair of edges. For nowhere-zero $A$-flows with $|A|\ge 4$, replacing vertices of degree more than $4$ by triangles reduces the problem to graphs with all degrees at most $4$. For integer flows, a counting argument joins any two nowhere-zero flows with values in the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_k$, $k\ge 4$, by changes that add $1$, $-1$, $2$ or $-2$; every such chain gives a chain of integer flows with values between $1$ and $k-1$ in absolute value, and every integer flow of this chain reduces modulo $k$ to a flow of the given chain. All results of this paper are also proved in the Lean 4 proof assistant, from Lean's standard axioms alone.
On the factorization graph of finite groups
Ismael Gutiérrez; Yesneri Zuleta y E. J. García-Claro

Given a finite group $G$, the factorization graph $Γ(G)$ has as vertices the nontrivial proper subgroups of $G$, with two distinct vertices $H$ and $K$ adjacent if and only if $HK = G$. In this paper, we study structural and combinatorial properties of $Γ(G)$ for three families of groups: cyclic groups of square-free order, generalized quaternion groups, and dicyclic groups. For cyclic groups $C_{p_1\cdots p_r}$, we describe the global structure of $Γ(G)$ and determine its order, degree sequence, center, girth, and diameter. We also characterize completely when $Γ(G)$ is claw-free, show that it is non-planar for $r \geq 4$, and prove that after removing all pendant vertices, the resulting induced subgraph is 2-connected; we further compute its exact circumference for small $r$, showing it is Hamiltonian precisely when $r=4, 5$. For generalized quaternion groups, we classify all isolated vertices and prove that the reduced factorization graph has diameter two and a unique central vertex. Moreover, we show that it is planar, has chromatic number~$3$, is Eulerian, and non-Hamiltonian, and that it contains maximal induced stars and triangular book subgraphs. Finally, we analyze the dicyclic case and show that the reduced factorization graph is a complete bipartite graph, from which all main invariants follow directly. An explicit SageMath algorithm for constructing $Γ(G)$ is included.
Generic properties of the Laplace spectrum and eigenfunctions
Oliver Fürst; Eva-Maria Hekkelman; Malte Leimbach

We prove that the spectrum of the Laplace--Beltrami operator on compact Riemannian manifolds without boundary is generically linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$. Furthermore, we prove that pointwise products of eigenfunctions generically are linearly independent. The proof is based on conformal perturbations of the metric. The result implies in particular that generically the truncation of the continuous functions on $M$ by spectral projections of the Laplace operator is given by symmetric matrices.

A finitely generated module has unbalanced support if its support has positive dimension but meets a top-dimensional component of the spectrum only at the closed point. We ask what homological signals are left behind by this geometry. Separating the spectrum into two wings, we prove first Tor nonvanishing for positive-depth modules and give criteria for second Tor nonvanishing. In depth zero, we obtain a structural sequence describing the finite-length torsion under a first Tor vanishing. A recent counterexample to the Peskine--Szpiro dimension inequality conjecture establishes the existence of modules of finite projective dimension and unbalanced support \cite{Ma}. We apply our framework to these modules and establish a numerical torsion--spine balance for linked Cohen--Macaulay wings. We also construct such modules over a reduced Gorenstein ring with exactly two irreducible components.
Simple proofs of a Gagliardo--Nirenberg inequality and their extensions

We revisit the one-dimensional Gagliardo-Nirenberg interpolation inequality $$\|u'\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R})}\leq C\|u\|_{L^q(\mathbb{R})}^{1-a}\|u''\|_{L^r(\mathbb{R})}^{a},\qquad u\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R}),\quad \tfrac12\leq a\leq 1,$$ and recall how its general form follows from the case $a=\frac12$ by interpolation with an endpoint estimate. For $a=\frac12$ and $p=q=r$, we give four alternative proofs, based on integration by parts (two proofs), on an ODE, and on the $L^p$ theory of singular integrals. The two proofs by integration by parts also cover most of the other admissible exponents. In $\mathbb{R}^N$, the integration by parts arguments give the inequality with explicit constants and, for $p\leq 2$, with the Laplacian in place of the Hessian and a constant independent of the dimension. For weighted measures $w(x)\,dx$, a pointwise version of the ODE argument gives the pointwise inequality $|\nabla u|^2\leq C_N\,Mu\,M(Δu)$, where $M$ is the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function, and hence the inequality for Muckenhoupt weights, with the Laplacian and an explicit constant. The integration by parts arguments give it for homogeneous weights of large degree and for superharmonic weights. These results apply, in particular, to power weights and to monomial weights.

Estimating biased finite-memory sources from a single trajectory is a fundamental problem with practical impact, for example in estimating entropy for cryptography. We study order-$d$ binary sources whose conditional probabilities have bias at most $ε$, and establish *sharp* sample complexity bounds: relative accuracy $γ$ with confidence $1-δ$ needs $γ^{-2}\,(\tfrac12-ε)^{-d}\,(\log d+\log\tfrac1δ)$ samples up to constants depending on $ε$, with matching upper and lower bounds and no dependence on mixing time or spectral gap. The proof rests on a sharp bound on expected hitting times of the sliding-window (de Bruijn) chain, which stay of order $1/π(w)$ uniformly in $d$ exactly when $ε<\tfrac3{10}$, and on majorization of the window masses by those of independent biased coins. Applied to published entropy-source validations, the bounds show that their trace lengths may be underpowered: $10^6$ bits cannot resolve all transitions of an $8$-bit model to better than about $4.5\%$ relative error.
The full shadow of a polynomial II. Vanishing root masses and holes

For a complex polynomial $P$, its full shadow is the closure of the set of zeros of all derivatives of all powers $P^n$, and its limiting core is the Hausdorff limit, as $n\to\infty$, of the set of zeros of all derivatives of $P^n$. These sets retain geometric information that weak limits of root-counting measures discard. We determine complete zero-set limits for arrays of polynomials whose roots approach finitely many locations. A cluster containing $o(D)$ roots of a degree-$D$ polynomial can survive outside the limiting support of the derivative zeros, which depends only on the positive limiting masses: under repeated differentiation, the zeros it produces follow a straight path, selected by an explicit min--max condition, and preserve the cluster's exact multiplicity. When such a location instead carries a small positive mass $\varepsilon$, the support of the limiting zero distribution at a fixed ratio of derivative order to degree develops an arc on the $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ scale with a universal local semicircle profile. We use these mechanisms to prove that polynomial shadows can have robust and arbitrarily complicated topology. For every $k\ge2$, there are polynomials with $k+2$ distinct root locations whose limiting cores and full shadows have at least $\binom{k}{2}$ holes; this persists under coefficient perturbations and among square-free polynomials without a reflection axis. In a four-location family, the core and full-shadow areas tend to zero while one hole has area tending to $8/1221$.
The nodally bound-preserving finite element method for the transport equation
Nicolás Espinoza-Contreras; Gabriel Barrenechea; Douglas Pacheco

Numerical approximations of transport problems, even when stabilised, often violate the bounds respected by the exact solution. Depending on the problem being solved, this can produce non-physical results, such as negative densities or higher-than-unity concentrations. Various bound-preserving numerical methods exist, yet they are usually either conditionally stable or only first-order accurate. In this context, the present work extends the nodally bound-preserving finite element method to the linear transport equation. As a baseline discretisation we use the least-squares finite element method, which is instrumental in achieving unconditional stability for second-order time stepping. It also leads to symmetric algebraic systems, thereby enabling simple, efficient solvers, which we further enhance through Anderson acceleration. Unconditional stability is proved for the backward Euler and Crank--Nicolson discretisations. We also derive error estimates for the fully discrete second-order scheme and provide various numerical examples, including two-phase incompressible flows.

In this paper, we first construct the dual of a representation of a pre-Leibniz algebra and study infinitesimal deformations of a pre-Leibniz algebra with a representation, which lead to Nijenhuis pairs, characterizing trivial deformations, and to dual-Nijenhuis pairs. Building on these notions, we introduce Kupershmidt-(dual-)Nijenhuis structures and show that they give rise to hierarchies of pairwise compatible Kupershmidt operators, the converse holding under an invertibility condition. Finally, we show that Rota--Baxter--Nijenhuis structures, $r$-$n$ structures and BN-structures all arise as particular cases, and that the first two correspond to each other on quadratic pre-Leibniz algebras.
An infinite family of conservation laws for perfect compressible fluids
Bruno Le Floch; Philippe G. LeFloch

We prove the existence of an infinite family of conservation laws and, more generally, balance laws, satisfied by plane-symmetric flows of perfect compressible fluids, allowing all components of the velocity vector to be possibly non-vanishing. We cover general pressure laws satisfying solely hyperbolicity and asymptotic conditions. We exhibit an almost quadratic formulation of the Euler equations, which we refer to as the J-formulation, and introduce a reduced Euler system based on an effective mass-energy density and an effective pressure law which account for transverse velocities. We establish the existence of a fundamental kernel which we use to generate all spacetime (quasi-)currents, also called mathematical entropy pairs. We derive explicit formulas for their density and flux components, together with the source-terms of the corresponding balance laws. Furthermore, we establish regularity and asymptotic estimates covering the whole range of physical variables, including vacuum. We prove that the kernel is positive on the interior of its support provided the pressure law satisfies a genuine nonlinearity condition, and we also investigate the future-convexity of the spacetime currents. Throughout, the fluid momentum parallel to the orbits of plane-symmetry is kept arbitrary. In turn, this family of spacetime quasi-currents provides a key ingredient in our companion study of torus-symmetric Einstein-Euler flows with weak regularity.
Sharp convex body sparse bounds and quantitative matrix weighted estimates for Hilbert transforms along curves

We prove convex body sparse bounds for coordinatewise Hilbert transforms along monomial curves and local $C^d$ curves with uniformly nonvanishing torsion on the closed integration interval. Adapting the scalar estimates of Cladek--Ou \cite{CladekOu2018} and the lifting method of Laukkarinen--Lorist \cite{LaukkarinenLorist2026} to the anisotropic geometry, we obtain one sparse family of genuine curve-adapted boxes and quantitative $L^p(W)$ bounds for matrix weights. The convex body sparse exponent range is sharp up to its boundary: estimates hold in the interior of $Ω_d$, while any fixed finite number of sparse families fails outside $\overline{Ω_d}$ when $1/r+1/s>1$. We also establish an explicit endpoint-contact obstruction. For every interior planar exponent pair, a polynomial curve with positive torsion on the open integration interval violates the full-interval sparse estimate.
A Local Fourier-Transform Proof of Offen's Spherical Transfer Theorem

Let $E/F$ be an unramified quadratic extension of non-archimedean local fields of characteristic zero and odd residual characteristic. Offen proved that, on the full spherical space of nondegenerate Hermitian matrices, equality of the Hironaka and Satake transforms implies Jacquet--Ye matching. We give a purely local proof of this theorem. The argument combines Jacquet's compatibility of matching with Fourier transform, the Godement--Jacquet functional equation, and Hironaka's scalar functional equation for Hermitian zeta integrals. The local proof recovers Jacquet's spherical-Hecke fundamental lemma from the unit case.
Integral Brauer--Manin Obstruction for Fermat Near Misses

We study the integral Hasse principle for the affine surfaces given by $x^4+y^4-w^2=m^2$, where $m>1$ is odd and squarefree. We give a criterion to determine if there is an integral Brauer--Manin obstruction, which depends only on simple congruence conditions on the prime factors of $m$ modulo $8$. We use this to show that for $100\%$ of such surfaces there is no integral Brauer--Manin obstruction to the Hasse principle for integral points.
Integral Hodge structures and atoms of fourfolds

Following the recent work by OpenAI on the irrationality of very general cubic fourfolds in Hassett divisors, we prove some compatibility of Iritani's blow-up formula with the classical blow-up decomposition of integral Hodge structures. As a consequence, we express OpenAI's birational invariant in terms of the theory of atoms developped by Katzarkov--Kontsevich--Pantev--Yu. We also show that, for every smooth complex rational cubic fourfold, the primitive cohomology is isometric as an integral Hodge structure to the twisted middle cohomology of a K3 surface and we prove irrationality of the very general Verra fourfold.
Tate and Artin--Tate Motivic Tensor-Triangular Geometry

We compute the Balmer spectra of geometric Tate and Artin--Tate motives with $\mathbb{F}_p$-coefficients over any field whose characteristic differs from $p$. For Tate motives, we find the bigraded comparison map to be a homeomorphism to the homogeneous spectrum of the motivic cohomology of the base field. For Artin--Tate motives, we describe the spectrum as a gluing of the spectrum of Artin motives computed by Balmer--Gallauer with the punctured Tate spectrum. We determine all specialisations between these pieces and the resulting topology. Under the hypothesis that the spectrum of rational Tate motives is a singleton, we also compute the integral Tate spectrum after inverting the exponential characteristic of the base field. As a consequence of our results, we identify the punctured Tate spectrum as an open subspace of the spectrum of the category of geometric Voevodsky motives, and draw some conclusions concerning the latter. Finally, we include an appendix where we define generalised periodicity in the context of tensor-triangular geometry, and explore its applications in motivic settings.
Heat trace and Riesz means with a large Robin parameter

We consider the Laplacian with Robin boundary conditions on a smooth Riemannian manifold with boundary and investigate the behavior of various spectral quantities as the Robin parameter approaches infinity. Although the spectrum, heat trace, and Riesz means converge pointwise to their Dirichlet analogues, the asymptotics of these quantities as the spectral parameter approaches infinity, or as time approaches zero, do not. The remainders in the usual asymptotic expansions are not bounded as the Robin parameter approaches infinity. Our main result is a two-term asymptotic expansion for the Robin heat trace that depends jointly on the time variable and the Robin parameter, with a remainder that satisfies a uniform bound independent of the Robin parameter. We apply this result to obtain a similar two-term asymptotic expansion for Riesz means of order at least one, again with a remainder bound independent of the Robin parameter.
Exotic involutions on irreducible 4-manifolds from Real Seiberg--Witten theory

Using Real Seiberg--Witten theory, Miyazawa constructed infinitely many exotic involutions on ${\overline{\mathbb{CP}}{}^2}$, and Baraglia extended this construction to $X\#{\overline{\mathbb{CP}}{}^2}$ for a broad class of $4$-manifolds $X$ equipped with an involution $c$. We show that, under suitable Real Seiberg--Witten hypotheses, the ${\overline{\mathbb{CP}}{}^2}$ summand can be omitted when $X$ is non-spin and the complement of the fixed locus is simply-connected. Our construction also yields infinite families of topologically isotopic but smoothly non-isotopic embeddings of the branch surface in the quotient $X/\langle c\rangle$. As applications, we construct anti-holomorphic involutions on irreducible, simply-connected projective surfaces of general type with infinitely many exotic copies, none of which is anti-symplectic with respect to any orientation-compatible symplectic form. These surfaces include cyclic branched covers of $\mathbb{CP}^2$ and complete intersections of multidegree $(2,4k)$ in $\mathbb{CP}^4$.
Monopole-Fermion Scattering from Twisted Conformal Boundary States
Clay Córdova; Diego García-Sepúlveda; Lian-Tao Wang; Yen-Chieh Wang

We derive monopole-fermion scattering correlators from conformal boundary states in twisted sectors. The key ingredient is that symmetry-preserving boundary conditions contain sectors twisted by topological symmetry lines. Their overlaps determine correlators of operators attached to these lines, including the outgoing excitations required by charge conservation in the Callan-Rubakov effect. We construct the twisted boundary states of $N$ free Dirac fermions with $U(1)^N$-preserving boundary conditions, extending the familiar description in terms of charge lattices to shifted lattices describing twisted sectors. Using cluster decomposition and open-closed duality, we determine their coefficients and fix their normalization relative to the untwisted boundary state. We find that the Callan-Rubakov boundary condition yields a two-point function between an incoming fermion and an outgoing defect operator with a coefficient of unit modulus, even when the corresponding correlators of ordinary local fermions vanish. Finally, we relate these correlators to four-dimensional partial-wave scattering using gauge-covariant asymptotic states. We identify the missing $s$-wave contribution to the unitarity relation and argue that the twisted channel supplies it with precisely the required normalization.
On Boundary State Screening via Solitons
Vivek Chakrabhavi; Babak Haghighat; Jonathan J. Heckman

We present a coarse classification scheme for the boundary data of massive QFTs based on transitions of boundary states via soliton / kink profiles. Starting from the lattice of boundary states, we introduce the boundary screening group $\mathbb{B}$: the equivalence classes of boundary states which cannot be connected by such transitions. In string theory backgrounds which geometrically engineer an interacting QFT in the target space, $\mathbb{B}$ computes the worldsheet analog of the target space defect group $\mathbb{D}$. When $\mathbb{B}$ is non-zero, it provides a diagnostic for having a target space with non-normalizable modes. For interfaces between QFTs, similar considerations imply the existence of a non-trivial conserved charge associated with soliton absorption / transmission, which means that the interface cannot fully dissolve / disappear. Similar considerations hold for junctions of QFTs, which in the special case of string worldsheet CFTs translate to junctions of string theories. We illustrate these general considerations with a number of non-geometric 2D $\mathcal{N} = (2,2)$ Landau-Ginzburg models, as well as their natural lifts to 4D $\mathcal{N} = 1$ Wess-Zumino models.
Systolic Geometry and Combinatorics of Surfaces

This thesis investigates two themes. The first studies systolic embeddings of graph on translation surfaces, proving existence results for essential and cellular systolic embeddings and determining extremal genera for certain graph families. The second examines hyperbolic surfaces in the Thurston set, constructing a one-parameter deformation that increases the sys- tole length and produces Bolza-like surfaces, i.e., surfaces whose systolic geodesics decompose the surfaces into triangles, for infinitely many genera. A symmetry property of geodesic inter- sections on these surfaces is also established, together with an application of these Bolza-like surfaces.
Homotopy in enriched functor categories: Frobenius exact structures and weak Serre functors

Let $(\V, \otimes, I,[-,-])$ be a closed symmetric monoidal category with finite (co)limits. Assume that $\V$ is weakly idempotent complete and additive. For a given small $\V$-category $\A$, we investigate sufficient conditions on $\A$ under which the ordinary category $[\A, \V]_0$ of $\V$-functors from $\A$ to $\V$, equipped with the exact structure $\mathcal{E}_{\textrm{lowt}}$, is a Frobenius exact category,and hence, induces a triangulated stable category. The exact structure $\mathcal{E}_{\textrm{lowt}}$ encompasses the degre-wise trivial exact structure on categories of $N$-chain complexes and $m$-periodic chain complexes, with terms in a variety of settings, including left $R$-modules, quasi-coherent sheaves on a scheme, and Banach spaces. We subsequently address the question of describing abstract left and right homotopy relations in $([\A, \V]_0;\mathcal{E}_{\textrm{lowt}})$ in terms of families of morphisms defined objectwise, as in the cases of chain-homotopy and relative homotopy relations. To this end, we introduce the notion of left/right-weak Serre $\V$-functors on $\A$, and investigate their relationships with the classical Serre functor relative to a commutative ring $k$.
Sharp Nonlocal Poincaré Inequalities and Liminf Lower Bounds for Sobolev and BV Energies on Metric Measure Spaces
Feng Dai; Tuomas P. Hytönen; Dachun Yang; Wen Yuan; Yirui Zhao

Let $p\in[1,\infty)$, and let $(X,ρ,μ)$ be a complete doubling $q$-Poincaré space for some $q\in[1,p]$ with a lower dimension $d$ and an upper dimension $D$. In this article, we establish Poincaré inequalities for two families of nonlocal nonconvex functionals defined using distances or volumes. More precisely, for any ball $B$ with its radius $r_B\in(0,\operatorname{diam} X)$, any $λ\in(0,\infty)$, and any measurable function $f:X\to\mathbb R$, \begin{align*} &\frac{1}{μ(B)^2}\int_B\int_B|f(x)-f(y)|^p\,dμ(x)\,dμ(y)\\ &\quad\lesssimλ^pr_B^pϕ(B)^{γp}+\frac{λ^pr_B^p}{μ(B)}\mathop{\int_{ΛB}\int_{ΛB}}\limits_{\genfrac{}{}{}{2}{|f(x)-f(y)|}{ρ(x,y)ϕ(x,y)^γ}>λ}\frac{ϕ(x,y)^{γp}}{V(x,y)}\,dμ(x)\,dμ(y), \end{align*} where $V(x,y):=μ(B(x,ρ(x,y)))$ and either $ϕ=ρ$ with $ϕ(B)=r_B$ and $γ\in(-\infty,-\frac{\min\{q,D\}}{p}]$ or $ϕ=V$ with $ϕ(B)=μ(B)$ and $γ\in(-\infty,-\frac{q}{p\max\{q,d\}}]$. Here both ranges of $γ$ are sharp over the class of $q$-Poincaré spaces with the prescribed lower and upper dimensions, and the constant $Λ\in[1,\infty)$ and the implicit positive constant depend only on $p$, $γ$, and the geometric constants of $X$. We also obtain lower bounds for Sobolev energy and total variation in terms of the limit inferior of these functionals, for $γ$ in either the above negative ranges or $(0,\infty)$. Our proofs use the curve characterization of Poincaré spaces and an adaptive dyadic refinement argument based on medians.
Pareto-Optimal Hypersonic Vehicle Design with Canonical-Coordinate Neural Operator Surrogates Under Ablation-Driven Shape Change and Incidence Variation
Khemraj Shukla; Jeremy Redding; Luis Bravo; George Em Karniadakis

High-fidelity CFD is essential for coupled hypersonic aerodynamic and aerothermal phenomena, but its cost precludes multi-objective design optimization. We develop three DeepONet surrogates for two hypersonic configurations, unified by one device: the trunk receives coordinates in which the varying feature is held fixed. The first is a prescribed family of 37 spherically blunted tangent ogives, varied through ogive radius of curvature to span nose-tip ablation forebody change; no ablation is computed. A body-fitted canonical transformation maps every domain onto a common (s, eta) space, retaining physical coordinates for forces and heat transfer. A branch network predicts reduced coefficients and a Transolver trunk with Physics-Attention learns the spatial basis; a two-step strategy optimizes both jointly, orthonormalizes the basis by QR factorization, and trains a second-stage branch for unseen geometries. Surrogates cover density, pressure, velocity, temperatures, conductivities and species mass fractions. In leave-one-out tests, drag, mean and peak wall heat flux are recovered to 1.16%, 1.62% and 5.29%; a sweep of 1001 geometries gives a 200-design Pareto front trading 6.68% in drag for 4.42% in peak heating (a diagnostic, not an objective). The second is the 3D AEDC waverider at 29 angles of attack: static mesh, moving leading-edge shock. For surface quantities, the same construction predicts integrated heat load within 0.22% and force coefficients to errors below 2.6x10^-5; Pareto fronts identify angles of attack trading drag, lift and heating. For the volume field, a Cartesian trunk smears the shock; a frozen ShockNet supplies a shock-aligned coordinate and a hotspot-aware mixture of experts corrects the residual, recovering density to 12.28% relative L2 error at a held-out incidence (5.08x10^7 nodes). The 1001-design sweep takes about three minutes on a single CPU.
On Some Special Cases of the Weber-Schafheitlin Integral

We consider special cases of the discontinuous Weber--Schafheitlin integral in which the orders $μ$ and $ν$ of the Bessel functions differ by an integer and the exponent $λ$ equals $0$ or $\pm1$, with $μ-ν+λ$ odd. Explicit closed-form results are obtained in terms of Jacobi polynomials.
SKFitter: Symmetry resolved Slater Koster tight-binding models from first principles for s, p, d and f electrons, spin orbit coupling and magnetism
Sundeep Kapila; Bhaskaran Muralidharan; Satadeep Bhattacharjee

Constructing accurate and physically interpretable tight binding (TB) Hamiltonians from first principles calculations remains challenging, particularly for materials exhibiting complex orbital hybridization, spin orbit coupling (SOC), and magnetic order. SKFitter is an open-source Python framework for constructing and optimizing symmetry resolved Slater Koster TB models directly from density functional theory (DFT) calculations performed using Quantum ESPRESSO or VASP. The framework supports s to f orbitals, incorporates on site SOC and site resolved magnetic exchange interactions, and accommodates both orthogonal and nonorthogonal basis. A central feature is the symmetry resolved parameterization of orbital manifolds, which allows independent two centre hopping integrals between symmetry allowed orbital groups and across distinct neighbour shells. SKFitter also identifies missing orbital contributions and guide systematic basis set refinement and optimizes parameters through weights. The resulting Hamiltonian can be used to evaluate anomalous (AHC) and spin Hall conductivities (SHC), and topological invariants. We demonstrate the framework using eight representative materials spanning semimetals, semiconductors, transition metals, f-electron compounds, and magnetic systems. Symmetry resolved models achieve band energy errors of 9 to 41 meV within 1 eV of the Fermi level. The fitted Hamiltonians reproduce characteristic features of the SHC response of Pt, the SOC dependence of the AHC of Fe, and the momentum dependent altermagnetic spin splitting of MnTe without any altermagnet specific interaction. For EuMn2Bi2, projection guided orbital refinement reduces the near Fermi level fitting error from 120 to 32 meV. Together, these results establish SKFitter as a flexible and reproducible framework for developing symmetry consistent, physically interpretable TB models of complex materials.

Let $p(n)$ be the minimum cardinality of a finite planar point set in which each point has exactly $n$ unit-distance neighbours. Harborth proved $p(5)=18$ in work presented in 1985 and published in 1987, using a detailed case analysis. We revisit the proof using convex-hull arguments, incidence counts, and elementary properties of intersections of unit circles. These tools give an alternative treatment of configurations with $14$ and $16$ points and organize the final case distinction by a common vector-sum structure. We also treat a configuration not explicitly covered by the case analysis in the online PDF copy of Harborth's paper available to us, and give an explicit justification of the six-point classification used in the argument. No result subsequent to Harborth's proof is required.
INLA for Adaptive UAV Sampling of Radio Environment Maps in IoT Networks: Prior Width Governs Accuracy and Calibration
Changhao He; Kaichuang Yang; Xiaojuan Zhang

We study adaptive UAV sampling for radio environment map (REM) construction from non-Gaussian IoT observations. Integrated nested Laplace approximation(INLA) updates a Matérn GMRF posterior, with waypoints selected by entropy pre-screening and Sherman--Morrison lookahead over the reachable set. We show that the likelihood-induced Skew-Normal correction has a sextic entropy effect, explaining its limited influence on waypoint selection. Across 19 retained ray-traced windows,Random and lawnmower sampling cost a median 18.0\% and 14.0\% more residual NMSE than posterior-informed sampling, equivalently reductions of 15.3\% and 12.3\% when referred to those baselines, while differences among informative rules remain unresolved. Widening the prior shadowing standard deviation from 6.0 to 10.025\,dB improves NMSE and credible-interval coverage, with monotone improvement over a 4--16\,dB sweep on this corpus and no observed turning point, although overconfidence persists. Online width estimation from the UAV's own counts yields about 6.5\,dB without recovering the gain. Across 30 measured LoRaWAN propagation windows paired with simulated counts and scored only on received cells, the margin over non-adaptive sampling reproduces, the training-derived width minimizes the tested interval score, and GP-UCB has nominally $3$--$5\%$ lower NMSE. The results show substantial, corpus-dependent sensitivity to prior specification, while fine differences among acquisition rules have limited or unresolved effects, the preferred width depends on the corpus, scored cells and model mismatch.
Bernstein and Stieltjes properties of some functions involving logarithmic functions

We show that $\frac1{g(x)}$, with $g(x)=\frac{x-1}{x\ln x}$, is a complete Bernstein function and give its Lévy measure explicitly. For $h(x)=\frac{(x^2-1)\ln(x+1)}{x^2\ln x}$, we prove that $h$ is not a Stieltjes function, so $\frac1h$ is not a complete Bernstein function, but $\frac1h$ is a Bernstein function. The latter rests on the positivity of a function built from the convolution of the exponential integrals $E_1$ and $E_2$. We also give a related completely monotonic function that is not a Stieltjes function.
The Geometry of Multitask Learning: Sharp Rates for Shared Subspace Estimation
Tony Cai; Abhinav Chakraborty; Samory Kpotufe

Learning a shared subspace in multitask learning is an important statistical problem, yet exact rates remain poorly understood in many of the formal settings considered in the literature. To address this gap, which arises from limitations of existing upper-bound techniques, we propose a general multitask lemma. The lemma provides sufficient conditions for fast subspace estimation in generic multitask settings, in the form of geometric conditions on the task regression functions and their estimators. We subsequently show that the multitask lemma yields sharp minimax rates---previously unknown---for linear regression and classification in the regimes considered, and rates matching up to logarithmic factors for additive-noise regression.
Anti-concentration and Graham's rearrangement problem in finite abelian groups
Hoi H. Nguyen; Tuan Tran; Van H. Vu

Let $S$ be a subset of $n$ elements of a group $G$. An ordering $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ of its elements is valid if the partial sums $x_1,x_1+x_2,\ldots,x_1+\cdots+x_n$ are pairwise distinct. This notion has a long history in combinatorial group theory, dated back to Gordon's works in early 1960. Alspach-Liversidge conjecture asserts that any subset of the nonzero elements of a finite abelian group $G$ has a valid ordering. This generalizes Graham's conjecture, which considers the case when the group $G$ is $\mathbb{F}_p$, the cyclic group of prime order. Graham's conjecture has been solved recently, as a combination of results by Kravitz, Bedert and Kravitz, Müyesser and Pokrovskiy, Bedert, Bucić, Kravitz, Montgomery, and Müyesser, and Pham and Sauermann. Beside this, the only other case where Alspach-Liversidge conjecture has been confirmed is $G=\mathbb{F}_2^k$, thanks to a recent result by Bedert, Bucić, Kravitz, Montgomery, and Müyesser. We prove the Alspach-Liversidge conjecture in its full generality. Our proof combines ideas from many previous papers. In particular, we will use the probabilistic approach and the absorption method. Our new main technical ingredient is a Fourier-moment estimate, which is of independent interest. In particular, we can use it to show that the distribution of certain kinds of random sums in an abelian group has an almost uniform distribution.
JT gravity as a conformal scaling limit of random flat combinatorial disks

We prove that flat Jackiw--Teitelboim (JT) gravity arises as a conformal scaling limit of random flat combinatorial disks. We give a clean criterion, formulated in terms of branching explorations, for a discrete model to converge to this conjecturally universal limit. For simplicity, we apply this criterion to a Boltzmann ensemble of disks with rectilinear boundary, defined by summing over combinatorial types and integrating over lengths. As the length of a distinguished side tends to infinity, the rescaled surface converges in law to a continuum random surface prescribed by Ferrari's path-integral formulation of JT gravity. Convergence is in the topology of smooth convergence of the conformal factors on compact subsets of the interior when uniformizing in a fixed domain; the limiting conformal factor is described by a harmonic Gaussian field closely related to holomorphic multiplicative chaos. The crux is a branching exploration of flat JT gravity whose lengths evolve as conditioned Cauchy processes and whose unexplored components are conditionally independent. We construct this exploration using a conformal welding theorem proved in a companion paper, and show that it is the scaling limit of Budd's row-by-row exploration of the discrete disks, analogous to the peeling of random planar maps. Under a tightness condition, our criterion upgrades this convergence to a conformal scaling limit for the discrete disks. Other natural combinatorial disk models admit analogous first-row recursions, providing a route to their scaling limits.
Multicomplexes in Action: Strong Formality of Compact Hyperkähler Manifolds

We show that all compact hyperkähler manifolds are bigraded strongly formal in the sense of Milivojević and Stelzig, proving that in the context of pluripotential homotopy theory they play the same role as compact Kähler manifolds in rational homotopy theory. Indeed, the main result arises from general algebraic considerations on categories of objects with more differentials, that of multicomplexes and commutative $n$-differential graded algebras. For them we discuss a standard model category structure, introduce a generalization of the $\partial\bar{\partial}$-Lemma and establish an algebraic formality theorem.
Central Limit Theorems and Network-Free Inference for Heterogeneous Spatial Autoregressions on Sparse Graphons

Network dependence is widely regarded as a fundamental obstacle to inference: outcomes linked through a graph are not independent, the graph is rarely observed in full, and models for how dependence propagates are easily misspecified. We show that for a broad class of responses generated through a random network, the obstacle is smaller than it appears. We study a heterogeneous spatial autoregression on a sparse graphon, in which each node's response is a weighted average of its neighbors' responses with a node-specific, nonparametric coefficient plus a node-specific input, and we prove that sample means and smooth functions of vector means are asymptotically Gaussian down to average degree nearly logarithmic in the population size, allowing unbounded graphons with hubs and heavy-tailed inputs. The limiting variance interpolates exactly between two regimes according to the sampling fraction. When the observed nodes are a vanishing fraction of the population, the variance is the marginal variance of the response, the ordinary sample variance is consistent, and the usual $t$-interval is valid with no knowledge of the network. The proof averages over the graph rather than conditioning on it, isolating the behavior of the response through an exact identity for resolvents of Markov kernels and controlling the network noise by an Efron-Stein inequality; neither step requires the walk-by-walk covariance bounds of fixed-network analyses. Consequences for regression with node-level and network-derived covariates are derived.
The Number of Tropical Order Types and Coherent Matching Fields
Xavier Allamigeon; Yiyuan Chen; Stéphane Gaubert; Xavier Goaoc

We investigate counting problems for discrete (geometric) structures in tropical settings, motivated by the comparison of the expressivity of linear programs and mean-payoff games. First, we give an upper bound on the number of coherent matching fields of type $(n,r)$ and a lower bound on the number of combinatorial types of $n$-hyperplane sequences in the max-plus tropical space of dimension $r-1$. These structures are closely related, and our bounds establish that as $n \to \infty$, for every fixed $r$ their number equals $n^{(r-1)^2n+o(n)}$. This in turn implies that the number of regular triangulations of the products of simplices $Δ^{n-1}\timesΔ^{r-1}$ is also $n^{(r-1)^2n+o(n)}$, thereby answering a question of Santos. Second, we obtain that the number of labeled order types over the reals and over the signed tropical numbers coincide at first order, establishing a comparison of the expressivity of mean-payoff games and linear programs as measured by labeled order types. Last, the subclass of mean-payoff games known as parity games arise from linear programs by a ``double tropicalization.'' We show that the number of labeled order types obtained after this double tropicalization collapses.

We study how curvature estimated from gradient differences can accelerate proximal-extragradient quasi-Newton methods. We introduce certified curvature reuse: one finite-difference probe per iteration refreshes a group of Hessian columns, while a path-length certificate controls the error of stale columns and determines the step. In the convex and strongly convex settings, bisection on stored scalar quantities selects a near-maximal certified stepsize; in the nonconvex setting, a uniform certificate gives an explicit learning rate. We prove a two-sided law of the iterated logarithm normalized by the full predictable quadratic variation \[ Q(x)=\sum_{p\le x}\bigg(\sum_{\substack{m\le x/p\\ P(m)<p}}f(m)\bigg)^2 \] of the martingale obtained by revealing the prime signs. Moreover, \[ \limsup_{x\to\infty} \frac{|M(x)|}{\sqrt{x}(\log\log x)^{1/4}} \] is either an almost surely finite and positive random variable with nondegenerate distribution or infinite almost surely. We study robust features of smooth surfaces in 4-space associated with contact with lines and hyperplanes. We investigate the local and multi-local singularities of orthogonal projections and height functions that describe these contacts and their corresponding geometric loci on the surface. At an $A_4$-singularity of a height function, we show that the $A_3$-curve and the $A_1A_2$-curve are generically tangent with contact of order $2$. We further establish criteria for the versality of the families of height functions and orthogonal projections in terms of the regularity of the $B_2$-curve and $S_2$-curve, respectively. Finally, we obtain the $[A_2]$- and $(A_0S_0)_2$-curves arising from multi-local singularities of orthogonal projections and describe their tangency properties at the $B_3$- and $H_3$-singularities.

A metric space admits an almost bi-Lipschitz embedding into a Euclidean space if and only if it is almost homogeneous. We prove the sufficient direction, complementing the known necessary condition. More quantitatively, we bound the target dimension and the embedding constants for every logarithmic exponent $γ>1$. Algebraic theory of abelian fractons and beyond
